Option.long:
An option is a contract giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a fixed strike price on or before an expiry date. The buyer pays a premium for that right; the seller collects the premium and takes on the matching obligation. Calls and puts are the two elemental forms, and everything more elaborate is assembled from them.

One equity contract typically covers 100 shares, so a quoted premium of 2.50 costs 250 dollars while controlling perhaps 15,000 dollars of stock. That gap between outlay and notional is the leverage, and also the trouble. An option's price splits into intrinsic value, from being in the money, and extrinsic value, the charge for time and expected movement.

Where people get fooled: the leverage feels symmetrical but the outcomes are not, because most bought options finish worth less than was paid. A trader can be right on direction and still lose through time decay or a fall in implied volatility. The premium is a price, set by a competitive market, not an entry fee.
Option.usage: Used whenever position risk is described in terms of premium paid rather than notional controlled, and as the parent term for every structure built from calls and puts.

Call.long:
A call is the right, not the obligation, to buy the underlying at the strike price before or at expiry. The buyer profits at expiry once the underlying trades above the strike by more than the premium paid; the seller keeps the premium and owes delivery above the strike.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. Stock at 100, a one-month 105 call bought for 2: expiry breakeven is 107, and anywhere below 105 the entire premium is gone. The stock can rise five per cent and the call buyer can still lose everything. Out-of-the-money calls are almost entirely extrinsic value, which means almost entirely a bet on speed as well as direction.

Where people get fooled: cheap-looking far out-of-the-money calls are priced from lottery odds, not generosity. A rally that arrives too slowly is claimed by theta, and a fall in implied volatility can offset a favourable move entirely. Being bullish and owning calls are related positions, not the same one.
Call.usage: Appears in any discussion of upside exposure with capped premium at risk, and as one leg of nearly every option structure.

Put.long:
A put is the right, not the obligation, to sell the underlying at the strike price. Its value rises as the underlying falls, which makes it the natural insurance contract: the buyer pays a premium for a floor, the seller underwrites the fall in exchange for that premium.

Stock at 100, a 95 put bought for 1.80: expiry breakeven is 93.20, and the stock must fall more than eight per cent from here before the position pays at expiry. Index puts carry persistently higher implied volatility than equivalent calls because portfolio protection is structurally in demand; that is the skew, and it is a price, not an error.

Where people get fooled: protection is most expensive immediately after the fall that made everyone want it. On average the put buyer pays implied volatility that exceeds what is subsequently realised, which is the variance risk premium working as designed. A slow grind lower can leave a put buyer right on direction and still down on the trade.
Put.usage: Used when describing downside insurance, bearish exposure with defined premium at risk, or the protective leg of hedged structures.

Strike.long:
The strike is the fixed price at which an option converts into the underlying if exercised. Each expiry lists a ladder of strikes, and the distance between spot and strike defines moneyness: in, at, or out of the money.

Strike selection is most of the trade. Nearer strikes cost more and pay off more often; distant strikes are cheap in dollars and expensive in probability. Delta gives a rough working proxy for the chance of finishing in the money, which makes it the honest way to compare strikes: a 0.10-delta option is priced as a long shot no matter how small the debit looks.

Where people get fooled: choosing strikes by dollar cost alone, as if a 30-cent option were a bargain rather than a statement of odds. Comparing premiums across strikes without looking at implied volatility and delta compares nothing. The strike that makes the story exciting and the strike that makes the arithmetic work are rarely the same one.
Strike.usage: Referenced when specifying any option position, and central to any comparison of cost against probability across a chain.

Premium.long:
The premium is the market price of the option, quoted per share and multiplied by contract size, so a quote of 3.40 on a standard equity contract costs 340 dollars. It decomposes into intrinsic value, the amount already in the money, and extrinsic value, the charge for time and expected movement.

The drivers are moneyness, time to expiry, implied volatility, interest rates and dividends. For the buyer, the premium is the maximum loss. For the seller, it is the entire compensation, whatever happens afterwards, which is why selling it obliges an honest look at what is being insured.

Where people get fooled: treating premium as a sunk admission fee rather than a price that can be rich or thin relative to what follows. A high premium is not an invitation; it usually means the market expects large movement, and sellers are being paid for genuine risk rather than gifted a yield. Comparing premiums without implied volatility context compares dollar amounts, not value.
Premium.usage: Used whenever the cost or credit of an option position is discussed, and when separating what was paid from what it was worth.

Moneyness.long:
Moneyness describes where the underlying sits relative to the strike. In the money means the option has intrinsic value now; at the money means strike and spot are close; out of the money means exercise would be pointless today and the entire premium is extrinsic.

Moneyness organises the greeks. At-the-money options carry the most extrinsic value, the highest gamma and the fastest theta; deep in-the-money options behave nearly like the underlying, with delta approaching 1.0; far out-of-the-money options are small, twitchy claims on rare outcomes. Delta doubles as a rough proxy for the probability of finishing in the money, which makes it a compact summary of moneyness and time together.

Where people get fooled: in the money is a statement about strike and spot, not about profit, which is measured against what was paid. Paths matter too: options frequently spend time in the money and still expire out of it, and only moneyness at expiry settles the contract.
Moneyness.usage: Used to locate an option on the strike ladder and to reason about which greeks dominate its behaviour.

Intrinsic value.long:
Intrinsic value is what exercising would collect right now: for a call, spot minus strike when positive, otherwise zero; for a put, strike minus spot. Stock at 110 makes a 100 call worth at least 10, because anything less is an arbitrage someone removes immediately.

Intrinsic is the floor under an option's price. Everything paid above it is extrinsic value, the charge for time and possible movement, and at expiry the extrinsic has gone and only intrinsic remains. This is why expiry is the moment of truth: the market's opinions about the future collapse into a single subtraction.

Where people get fooled: out-of-the-money options have zero intrinsic value, so their entire price is a wasting claim on movement that has not happened yet. And an option showing healthy intrinsic value can still be a losing trade if more was paid for it than it now returns. Intrinsic measures the contract against the market, not the trade against its cost.
Intrinsic value.usage: Used when decomposing an option's price, and when judging what a position would settle for at expiry.

Extrinsic value.long:
Extrinsic value is the premium minus intrinsic value: the part of the price paying for time and potential movement rather than value exercisable today. It is largest at the money, shrinks toward deep in- and out-of-the-money strikes, and reaches zero at expiry without exception.

Two forces govern it. Theta measures its decay through time, which accelerates as expiry approaches. Vega measures its response to implied volatility, which can inflate or crush it independent of the underlying's direction. An out-of-the-money option is entirely extrinsic, which is to say entirely a rented claim on future movement.

Where people get fooled: buying options that are mostly extrinsic and then holding while nothing happens, which is paying rent on an empty property. The move has to be large and reasonably prompt, or the decay collects. Cheap out-of-the-money options look like small risks; they are actually concentrated extrinsic value with an expiry date, and the usual outcome is quiet evaporation.
Extrinsic value.usage: Used when explaining why an option lost value despite the underlying cooperating, and when weighing time decay against expected movement.

Option delta.long:
Delta has two readings that make it the most used greek. First, sensitivity: the expected change in option price for a one-dollar move in the underlying, so a 0.30-delta call gains roughly 30 cents on a one-dollar rally. Second, a rough working proxy for the probability of finishing in the money, which turns the chain's deltas into a crude odds board.

Delta is not fixed. It rises and falls as spot moves, which is gamma; it drifts as time passes, which is charm; and it shifts as implied volatility changes, which is vanna. Summing deltas across a book gives position delta, the net directional exposure.

Where people get fooled: reading the probability proxy as precise, when it is model-dependent, ignores drift and skew, and moves constantly. A position hedged to zero delta today is not hedged tomorrow, or after a two-dollar move. Delta describes the current tangent, and markets do not travel along tangents for long.
Option delta.usage: Quoted whenever directional exposure of an option position is discussed, and used as a shorthand for the market-implied odds of a strike.

Gamma.long:
Gamma is the rate of change of delta for a one-dollar move in the underlying: the curvature of an option's exposure. Long option holders are long gamma, meaning delta bends in their favour as the market moves; short option holders bleed the other way, their losses accelerating into an adverse move.

Gamma peaks at the money and near expiry. An at-the-money option in its final hours can swing from a delta near 0.5 to nearly 1 or nearly 0 on a small move, which is why expiry weeks feel violent to anyone short them. Long gamma is not free: its daily cost is theta, and the position only pays if realised movement exceeds what was priced.

Where people get fooled: short gamma feels comfortable for weeks and then dominates a single afternoon. Sellers who size positions on quiet-market behaviour discover that the same contract's risk profile near expiry is a different animal. The smoothness before the event is not evidence about the event.
Gamma.usage: Used when explaining why option risk concentrates near the money and near expiry, and when describing dealer hedging behaviour.

Theta.long:
Theta is the daily erosion of an option's extrinsic value with everything else held still, quoted per day. The buyer pays it; the seller collects it. It is the metered price of holding a claim on movement that has not happened yet.

Decay is not linear. It accelerates as expiry approaches, fastest for at-the-money strikes: a 60-day option loses a little per day, the same strike with six days left loses a lot. This is also exactly when gamma is largest, because the acceleration of decay and the acceleration of risk are the same fact seen from opposite sides of the trade.

Where people get fooled: theta collected is often described as rent, as if the seller owned an asset. It is closer to an insurance premium: frequent small wins that are the scheduled compensation for rare large payouts the seller has promised to fund. Counting the theta without pricing the tail is underwriting without reserves, and it reads as skill right up until the claim arrives.
Theta.usage: Used when accounting for the daily cost of long options or the daily accrual of short ones, never in isolation from the risk being carried.

Theta decay curve.long:
The theta decay curve traces how extrinsic value erodes as expiry approaches. For at-the-money options the path is slow far from expiry and then steepens sharply in the final weeks and days, which is the familiar textbook curve. In- and out-of-the-money strikes hold less extrinsic to begin with and shed it earlier and flatter.

The textbook drawing assumes implied volatility holds still, which it does not. IV shifts move the whole curve up and down daily, events put kinks in it, and weekends compress three days of decay into pricing that adjusts before Friday's close. The curve is a useful average over conditions that individually never match it.

Where people get fooled: applying the at-the-money curve to every strike, when an out-of-the-money option may have done most of its decaying already. And selling the steep end of the curve to harvest the fastest decay means simultaneously holding the largest gamma, because the acceleration of decay and of danger arrive together, by construction.
Theta decay curve.usage: Referenced when timing entries and exits around decay, and when explaining why short-dated premium selling concentrates both yield and risk.

Vega.long:
Vega is the sensitivity of an option's price to a one-point change in implied volatility: an option showing 0.15 of vega gains about 15 cents per share if IV rises a point, and loses the same if it falls. Vega is largest at the money and grows with time to expiry, so long-dated options are substantially volatility instruments.

Long options are long vega, short options are short it. For positions beyond a few weeks, the IV component of profit and loss routinely rivals or exceeds the directional one, which surprises anyone who thought they were simply long or short the underlying.

Where people get fooled: being right on direction and losing on vega, the classic version being options bought just before a scheduled event at peak IV, then crushed when the uncertainty resolves. A long-dated call is a volatility trade wearing a directional costume, and the costume comes off whenever implied volatility moves faster than the stock does.
Vega.usage: Used when separating volatility exposure from directional exposure in any option position, especially longer-dated ones.

Rho.long:
Rho is the sensitivity of an option's price to a change in interest rates. Higher rates raise call values and lower put values through the cost of carrying the underlying: financing the forward becomes more expensive, and the strike's present value falls. For short-dated retail positions rho is usually the smallest greek on the sheet.

It stops being ignorable at longer maturities. Multi-year options carry meaningful rate exposure, and a moving rate cycle can shift their value materially with the underlying unchanged. Dividends work alongside rates in the same machinery, pulling call and put values in opposite directions.

Where people get fooled: apparent mispricings between calls and puts at the same strike are usually rates, dividends and borrow fees doing exactly what put-call parity says they should, not opportunity. And holders of long-dated options sometimes attribute a slow bleed to theta when a repricing of rates did the damage. Small most of the time is not the same as never material.
Rho.usage: Mentioned mainly for long-dated options and for explaining call-put price differences that trace to carry rather than opinion.

Implied volatility.long:
Implied volatility is the volatility number that makes a pricing model reproduce an option's market price. It is not measured from the underlying; it is backed out from what buyers and sellers agreed to trade at. That makes it a price, set by supply and demand for protection and leverage, not a forecast that comes true.

On average, implied runs above the volatility subsequently realised. That persistent gap is the variance risk premium: the margin option sellers charge for underwriting rare large losses, the same way insurers price policies above expected claims.

Where people get fooled: treating IV as a prediction, in either direction. Buyers assume high IV means a big move is certain; sellers assume high IV means options are overpriced and collecting is free money. Both miss that IV is high because informed participants are paying up for protection, often with reason. The number tells you what movement costs to insure today, not what movement arrives tomorrow.
Implied volatility.usage: Quoted whenever option prices are compared across strikes, expiries or time, and whenever richness or cheapness of premium is debated.

Realised volatility.long:
Realised volatility is what actually happened: the annualised standard deviation of the underlying's returns over some window. It is computed from history, so it is backward-looking by construction, and the choice of window and sampling frequency changes the number materially. Thirty days of daily closes and thirty days of five-minute bars describe the same month differently.

Volatility also clusters. Quiet regimes persist, violent regimes persist, and the transition between them is abrupt rather than announced. A low realised reading is a fact about the recent past and a weak statement about the future.

Where people get fooled: projecting recent realised volatility forward as if it were a property of the asset rather than of the sample. Option sellers sizing positions during a calm stretch are calibrating on precisely the data least representative of what hurts them. The comparison that settles accounts is not realised against memory but realised against what implied volatility had priced, measured after the fact.
Realised volatility.usage: Used as the after-the-fact benchmark against which implied volatility, and any volatility-selling result, is honestly judged.

Variance risk premium.long:
The variance risk premium is the persistent average gap between implied volatility and the volatility subsequently realised. Option sellers collect it; option buyers pay it. It has survived decades of being publicly documented, which is the strongest hint that it is compensation rather than error.

What it compensates is the tail. A seller's book looks like an insurer's: a long sequence of small premiums punctuated by occasional catastrophic claims when realised volatility explodes past what was priced. The premium exists because bearing that profile is genuinely unpleasant and periodically ruinous, and markets pay for what participants would rather not hold.

Where people get fooled: mistaking the collection phase for skill. Strategies harvesting the premium produce smooth equity curves that conceal the risk entirely until it detonates, and the average gap says nothing about the episodes that repay years of collection in days. Treating the premium as a market inefficiency to exploit, rather than a wage for carrying tail risk, is how the wage becomes a debt.
Variance risk premium.usage: Invoked to explain why selling options is profitable on average and why that average is not the whole story.

IV rank / IV percentile.long:
IV rank and IV percentile normalise current implied volatility against its own trailing year, because raw IV is incomparable across products: 30 is sleepy for a small-cap biotech and alarming for an index. Rank places today's reading within the year's high-low span; percentile counts the fraction of days that were lower.

The two can disagree sharply. A single extreme spike stretches the range and drags rank down for months while percentile barely notices, so a product can sit at a low IV rank and a high IV percentile simultaneously. Knowing which one a screen is quoting is not optional.

Where people get fooled: reading a high rank as a standing instruction to sell premium. IV can remain elevated, or go higher, and a regime change resets the entire lookback so the year defining the scale may resemble nothing that follows. These are ranking tools for comparison, not signals, and the base year is always the assumption doing the quiet work.
IV rank / IV percentile.usage: Used to compare current option pricing against its own history and across unrelated products on a common scale.

IV crush.long:
IV crush is the abrupt repricing of implied volatility once a scheduled uncertainty resolves: earnings, a trial result, a central bank decision. The event premium that accumulated in the option leaves it within minutes of the announcement, whatever the underlying does.

The crush is priced in advance, not sprung. A pre-earnings straddle costs what it costs precisely because everyone knows the stock tends to jump; the buyer only profits if the actual move exceeds the priced expected move, and the seller wears the excess when it does. The IV drop is not an anomaly, it is the schedule working as intended.

Where people get fooled: buying options before earnings because the stock always moves on earnings. The market agrees, and has charged for it. The stock gaps five dollars in the right direction and the option still opens lower, because the volatility component fell further than the intrinsic component rose. Direction was right; the trade was against the priced move, and lost.
IV crush.usage: Cited when option prices fall sharply through an event despite a favourable move in the underlying.

Volatility skew.long:
Volatility skew is the pattern of implied volatility differing across strikes at the same expiry. In equity indices, out-of-the-money puts trade at persistently higher IV than out-of-the-money calls, a tilt that has been present since the 1987 crash taught the market what left tails cost.

The mechanism is demand and asymmetry. Portfolio protection is structurally bid, crashes are faster than rallies, and return distributions carry a fat left tail that the lognormal model underneath a flat-volatility world does not. Skew is the market pricing those facts strike by strike. Its steepness moves with positioning and fear, which makes it informative about hedging demand.

Where people get fooled: reading skew as mispricing to fade. Selling the expensive puts is selling crash insurance at the going rate, and the extra premium is the payment for the exact scenario in which the seller is carried out. The tilt has persisted for nearly four decades; the traders who bet it was an error have not.
Volatility skew.usage: Referenced when comparing IV across strikes, and when explaining why downside protection costs more than symmetric models suggest.

Term structure.long:
Term structure is implied volatility plotted across expiries. In calm markets it usually slopes upward, longer-dated options carrying higher IV, since more time holds more room for surprise. In stress it inverts: front-month IV spikes above the back months because the uncertainty is here, now, and the market expects it to fade.

Scheduled events put visible bulges in the curve, with the expiry containing an earnings date or policy decision priced above its neighbours. Read this way, the structure is a map of when the market expects movement, expressed in prices rather than forecasts.

Where people get fooled: calendar trades built on the assumption that the curve normalises on a convenient schedule, when inversion is information about present conditions rather than a promise about next month. And judging a front-month IV as high against a long-run average, without noticing where on the curve it sits, compares a stressed point to a calm line and calls the difference opportunity.
Term structure.usage: Used when choosing expiries, pricing calendar structures, or reading which dates the market has flagged as eventful.

0DTE.long:
0DTE means zero days to expiry: options in their final session. Every property that builds gradually elsewhere is at its extreme here. Extrinsic value evaporates by the hour rather than the day, and gamma is at its sharpest, with delta snapping between near 0 and near 1 as price crosses the strike.

The dollar amounts look benign, which is the sales pitch. A cheap same-day option is small in absolute terms, enormous in annualised cost, and a large share of index option volume now trades in this form on both sides.

Where people get fooled: small debits disguise how often the entire debit vanishes by the close, and repeated daily the small losses compound into a substantial bleed. On the short side the trade collects pennies against intraday gap risk with no time left to be wrong, which is the short-volatility tail compressed into hours: frequent small wins, and the occasional afternoon that erases weeks of them.
0DTE.usage: Used when discussing same-day expiry trading and the concentration of gamma and decay into single sessions.

Assignment.long:
Assignment is the seller's side of exercise: the obligation arriving. When a holder exercises, a short is selected and must deliver or take the underlying at the strike. American-style options can be assigned on any day, and in practice it clusters where it is rational: deep in-the-money options with little extrinsic left, and calls the day before an ex-dividend date worth more captured than held.

Assignment converts an option position into a stock position overnight, with the margin consequences that implies. Spreads are not immune: one leg can be assigned while the other stays open, leaving exposure the original structure never contained.

Where people get fooled: assuming assignment only happens at expiry. The short leg of a defined-risk spread assigned early can briefly create a stock position far larger than the account behind it, and dividend dates are the recurring trap for anyone short calls on dividend payers. The risk is administrative in appearance and very real in effect.
Assignment.usage: Discussed whenever short options are held, particularly around dividends, deep in-the-money strikes and multi-leg structures.

Exercise.long:
Exercise is the holder's act of converting an option into the underlying position at the strike: calls take delivery, puts make it. At expiry, in-the-money options past a small threshold are typically exercised automatically unless the holder instructs otherwise.

Before expiry, exercising is usually the wrong arithmetic. An option sold in the market returns intrinsic plus remaining extrinsic value; an option exercised returns intrinsic only, so early exercise burns whatever time value remains. The rational exceptions are narrow and mechanical: calls just before a dividend that exceeds the remaining extrinsic, and deep in-the-money puts where the interest on the strike proceeds outweighs it.

Where people get fooled: exercising to take the stock out of sentiment and torching time value in the process, when selling the option and buying the shares separately keeps it. And forgetting auto-exercise, then discovering on Monday that a forgotten in-the-money contract became a leveraged stock position over the weekend. The sell-or-exercise decision is a subtraction, not a preference.
Exercise.usage: Used when describing settlement mechanics and the arithmetic of converting options into stock versus selling them.

Pin risk.long:
Pin risk is what a short option seller faces when the underlying closes expiry at or very near the strike. Whether the option is exercised depends on decisions the seller cannot see, made after the close, sometimes on the basis of after-hours moves. Until the notices arrive, the seller does not know whether they own stock, owe stock, or are flat.

The uncertainty spans the weekend. Whatever position materialises appears on Monday, unhedged through everything that happened in between, and the size can be the full contract amount per lot rather than the modest premium that was collected.

Where people get fooled: treating an at-the-strike expiry as a flat book. Contracts sitting a few cents either side of the strike get exercised or abandoned unpredictably, and the tidy assumption that it expired worthless fails exactly where the largest open interest tends to congregate. The premium seller's worst Friday close is not far from the strike but on it.
Pin risk.usage: Raised when short options approach expiry near the strike, and when explaining weekend exposure from unresolved assignment.

Open interest (options).long:
Open interest is the number of contracts outstanding at a given strike and expiry: positions currently open, as distinct from volume, which counts trading. It rises when new positions are created on both sides and falls when they are closed or exercised away.

Every contract has a long and a short, so open interest carries no direction by itself. A hundred thousand contracts at a strike says positioning is concentrated there; it does not say which way anyone is leaning, and much of it is hedged, spread against other strikes, or left over from trades whose purpose has passed. Its practical importance runs through dealer hedging: heavily held strikes anchor hedging flows as expiry approaches.

Where people get fooled: reading a large open interest strike as a wall or a target in its own right. The number describes where positions sit, not what anyone intends, and stories built on open interest alone are stories about a ledger. Mechanism arrives only when someone has to hedge.
Open interest (options).usage: Used to gauge where option positioning concentrates and to judge liquidity at a strike, never as a directional reading by itself.

Gamma exposure.long:
Gamma exposure, often abbreviated GEX, is an estimate of the aggregate gamma sitting on dealer books, inferred from outstanding options. It matters because hedging behaviour differs by sign. Dealers long gamma hedge by selling into rallies and buying into dips, which dampens movement; dealers short gamma must hedge with the move, buying strength and selling weakness, which amplifies it.

The mechanism is real and occasionally visible around large expiries. The measurement is another matter: the estimates require assumptions about which side of every trade dealers hold, published versions disagree, and the sign of the aggregate matters more than any decimal of the level.

Where people get fooled: precision theatre. Strike-by-strike gamma levels get quoted like engineering tolerances from a model whose core input, who holds what, is a guess. Treat the framework as a lens on why some regimes are sticky and others slippery, not as a level system, and note that regime flips arrive without a notification.
Gamma exposure.usage: Used when reasoning about whether dealer hedging is likely damping or amplifying index moves, with appropriate scepticism about the inputs.

Gamma squeeze.long:
A gamma squeeze is a feedback loop. Concentrated buying of short-dated calls leaves dealers short those calls; they hedge by buying stock. If price rises, the calls' deltas rise, requiring more stock bought, pushing price further, raising deltas again. The hedging is mechanical, which is what gives the loop its force.

The conditions are specific: heavy volume in near-dated out-of-the-money calls, thin underlying liquidity, and dealers predominantly on one side. The 2021 meme-stock episodes are the documented reference case, and their aftermath demonstrated the other half: the loop runs equally hard in reverse as deltas collapse and hedges unwind.

Where people get fooled: labelling every sharp rally a gamma squeeze, which converts a specific mechanism into a mood. And participating on the call-buying side means paying peak implied volatility to fund the squeeze; plenty of traders who described the mechanism accurately still lost money to the premiums, the crush afterwards, and the unwind they did not sell into.
Gamma squeeze.usage: Used for rallies plausibly amplified by dealer call hedging, with the burden of evidence on the specific conditions being present.

Max pain.long:
Max pain is the strike at which the aggregate value of expiring options is lowest for holders, and the attached theory says price drifts toward that point into expiry, to the maximum discomfort of option buyers. It is simple to compute from open interest, which is much of its popularity.

The evidence is weak relative to how confidently it is quoted. Where expiry-day pinning genuinely occurs, dealer hedging around heavily held strikes explains it through actual mechanics, no intent required, and that mechanism sometimes points to a different strike than the max pain calculation does.

Where people get fooled: selective memory does the marketing. The number is recalled loudly on the expiries where price landed nearby and never mentioned on the many where it did not, and no one keeps the score that would settle it. A price magnet with no funded mechanism behind it is a pattern in search of a cause, quoted with a precision the data does not support.
Max pain.usage: Mentioned when expiry-week price behaviour is discussed; the stronger mechanical explanation usually runs through dealer hedging instead.

Covered call.long:
A covered call is long stock with a call sold against it. The premium is kept whatever happens; upside beyond the strike is surrendered; the downside remains the stock's, cushioned only by the premium collected. Named honestly, it is a short-volatility profile: it converts uncertain large gains into certain small ones and keeps the large losses.

The pattern of outcomes follows: frequent modest premium collections, punctuated by rallies given away above the strike and slides absorbed nearly in full. Equity returns are lumpy, concentrated in a minority of strong months, and a standing covered call systematically sells precisely those months at a fixed price.

Where people get fooled: the premium framed as income from an asset, when it is the sale price of the stock's best outcomes. Frequent small wins with the occasional large forfeit or drawdown is the honest description, and over full cycles the drag from capped rallies plus retained downside is the real cost of the yield on the statement.
Covered call.usage: Described when discussing yield-generation overlays on stock positions and their true exchange of upside for premium.

Protective put.long:
A protective put is long stock plus a long put: insurance with the premium stated up front. Losses are floored near the strike for the life of the put, upside is retained, and the cost is the premium plus the puts that expire unused, which is most of them.

By put-call parity, stock plus put behaves like a call: the structure has simply made the insurance explicit. The recurring expense is the point. Implied volatility persistently runs above realised, so rolling protection pays the insurer's margin every cycle, and downside skew makes puts the most expensively insured corner of the market.

Where people get fooled: buying protection immediately after the fall, at peak implied volatility, then letting it lapse once calm returns, which is paying the most to hold it during the least. A permanent hedge quietly consumes returns; an occasional hedge requires the timing skill the hedge was supposed to replace. Insurance is a cost centre, and pretending otherwise is how it becomes a large one.
Protective put.usage: Used when discussing explicit downside insurance on a holding and the recurring cost of maintaining it.

Vertical spread.long:
A vertical spread is one option bought and another sold, same type and expiry, different strikes. The short leg's premium offsets part of the long leg's cost, and both maximum profit and maximum loss are fixed at entry. Debit and credit spreads are the same structure entered from opposite directions.

The arithmetic states the trade-off plainly. A five-point-wide spread sold for 1.00 collects 100 dollars against a maximum loss of 400: priced to win often and to lose several multiples of the win when it fails. The market sets that ratio from the same probabilities the seller is betting on.

Where people get fooled: quoting how often the trade wins without the payoff ratio beside it. A credit spread that succeeds in most months and occasionally loses the full width is a short-volatility profile in miniature, frequent small wins against rare larger losses, and the credit received is the market's estimate of exactly that exchange. Defined risk defines the loss; it does not shrink it.
Vertical spread.usage: Used for defined-risk directional positions and as the building block of condors, butterflies and boxes.

Straddle / strangle.long:
A straddle is a long call and long put at the same strike; a strangle uses out-of-the-money strikes on each side, costing less and needing more. Both are positions on movement in either direction: the buyer profits only if the underlying travels further than the combined premium, which is to say further than the market already priced.

The short versions collect both premiums and carry risk on both sides, open-ended beyond the strikes: the classic profile of frequent small wins and rare large losses, doubled.

Where people get fooled: buying straddles into known events, where the expected move is already in the price and the post-event IV crush claims much of the premium even when the underlying jumps. Knowing the event matters is not edge; the market knows too, and charged accordingly. Selling strangles because nothing has happened lately is the mirror error, sizing the quiet months as if they were evidence about the loud one that ends the sample.
Straddle / strangle.usage: Used for pure volatility positions, long or short, where direction is not the thesis and priced movement is the benchmark.

Iron condor.long:
An iron condor is a short out-of-the-money call spread stacked on a short out-of-the-money put spread, same expiry: a defined-risk bet that price stays inside a range. The structure collects one credit, and the wings cap the loss at the spread width minus that credit.

It is a short-volatility profile and should be described as one: it wins frequently and modestly while realised movement stays below what implied priced, and loses several multiples of the credit when price runs through either side. A condor collecting 1.00 on five-point wings risks 4.00, so a single breach can consume months of collections.

Where people get fooled: quoting the frequency of winning months without the payoff ratio attached, which is the win-rate illusion in structured form. Adjustment rules mostly redistribute losses rather than remove them, and sizing up after a calm year is calibrating on the sample that excludes the event. The wings define the catastrophe; they do not make it unlikely.
Iron condor.usage: Used for range-bound premium selling with capped tails, judged honestly only with payoff ratio alongside frequency.

Short volatility.long:
Short volatility is any position that profits when realised movement stays below what implied volatility priced: short options, credit spreads, iron condors, covered calls, inverse volatility products. The underlying engine is the variance risk premium, the persistent average gap between implied and realised that exists as compensation for rare large losses.

The return signature is unmistakable once named: a smooth, steadily rising equity curve punctuated by abrupt cliffs. February 2018 provided the canonical documented example, when a spike in volatility terminated a major inverse-VIX product in a single session after years of strong returns.

Where people get fooled: reading the smoothness as safety, when the strategy's entire risk lives in the tail its own track record has not yet displayed. Frequent small wins are the premium; the rare large loss is the claim being insured against, and it is not optional. Anyone selling volatility is running an insurance book, and the honest question is whether the reserves exist and whether the premium was adequate.
Short volatility.usage: Used as the umbrella term for premium-selling profiles, naming the shared risk shape that individual strategy labels obscure.

VIX.long:
The VIX is an index of roughly 30-day implied volatility extracted from S&P 500 option prices. It is best read as the current price of index protection: what insurance against near-term movement costs today. It is not a fear gauge in any mystical sense, and it is not directly tradable.

Exposure comes through futures and options on the index, and those instruments have their own term structure and basis. Spot VIX and the tradable products routinely part ways: futures usually sit above spot in calm markets and below it in panics, and the difference is where much of the profit and loss actually happens.

Where people get fooled: buying VIX ahead of the crash through products that bleed roll cost while waiting, so the crash must arrive promptly and violently to overcome the carry. Mean reversion in the index is real, but the tradable instruments already price it, and the timing owns the outcome. Both chronic longs and casual shorts have well-documented graveyards.
VIX.usage: Quoted as the standard reference for index option pricing levels and as context for volatility regime discussions.

Volatility ETP decay.long:
Volatility exchange-traded products cannot hold spot VIX, so they hold futures and roll them on a schedule. When the futures curve is in contango, which is most of the time, each roll sells the cheaper expiring contract and buys the dearer next one, a structural bleed that compounds relentlessly. Leveraged and inverse versions add decay from daily resets on top.

The long-term charts of long-volatility ETPs trend down and to the right with occasional violent spikes, which attracts two crowds: buyers who want the spike and shorts who want the trend. February 2018 settled the argument for one inverse product, which was terminated after a single session's spike.

Where people get fooled: shorting the obvious decay is itself a short-volatility profile, the smooth decline is the premium and the overnight spike is the claim. Borrow costs, buy-ins and forced covering arrive precisely when the trade is working worst. The decay is real; harvesting it safely is the part the chart does not show.
Volatility ETP decay.usage: Cited when explaining why volatility products underperform spot VIX over time and why both sides of them carry documented risks.

Calendar spread.long:
A calendar spread sells a near-dated option and buys a longer-dated one at the same strike. The near leg decays faster, which is the engine: the position profits if the underlying stays near the strike while the short leg's extrinsic value drains ahead of the long leg's.

The greeks describe its true character: short near-term gamma, long back-month vega. It is hurt by a large move in either direction, which drags both legs toward intrinsic value, and it is sensitive to the deferred expiry's implied volatility, which can fall and take the long leg's value with it even while the spot price cooperates.

Where people get fooled: modelling the trade on decay alone, as if the two thetas were the whole story. Term structure shifts and gaps through the strike dominate real outcomes, and an event that crushes back-month IV hits the leg that was supposed to be the anchor. The tidy sell-fast-decay picture assumes a stillness the position is implicitly betting on.
Calendar spread.usage: Used for positions on time decay differentials and term structure, with the strike doubling as a view on where price sits at the near expiry.

Diagonal spread.long:
A diagonal spread combines different strikes and different expiries: a calendar with a directional lean. The common form buys a longer-dated option and sells a shorter-dated one further out of the money, collecting near-term decay while keeping some of the long leg's exposure. The poor man's covered call is the household example.

The greeks are a blend: the short leg contributes theta and gamma risk near its expiry, the long leg contributes vega and direction. Payoff diagrams drawn at the short leg's expiry conceal the structure's real open question, which is what the long leg is worth at that moment.

Where people get fooled: treating the position as fully defined when the long leg's value at the short leg's expiry depends on implied volatility then, which is unknowable now. A vol crush can undercut the diagram's promised floor. Early assignment on the short leg converts the picture into a different trade overnight, and rolling the short leg is a sequence of new decisions, not a strategy on autopilot.
Diagonal spread.usage: Used for structures mixing time decay collection with a directional or volatility view across expiries.

Butterfly.long:
A butterfly uses three strikes: long one option below, short two at the middle, long one above, all the same type and expiry. Risk is defined on both sides, and the maximum payoff lands if the underlying settles exactly at the centre strike at expiry. It is cheap to enter precisely because that landing is unlikely.

The arithmetic advertises the odds. A ten-point-wide butterfly bought for 1.00 can pay up to 9.00 at the pin, and the market offering nine-to-one is stating its estimate of the probability, not misplacing a decimal. Away from the body, the position expires worthless and the debit is the loss.

Where people get fooled: reading the payoff multiple as edge rather than as the price of a low-probability outcome. Three legs mean three bid-ask spreads, which quietly consume much of the theoretical value on entry and exit. And the centre strike is a point forecast wearing a structure's clothing; the structure defines the risk, it does not improve the guess.
Butterfly.usage: Used for defined-risk positions targeting a specific settlement area, priced explicitly as a low-probability, high-multiple claim.

Ratio spread.long:
A ratio spread uses unequal legs, most commonly buying one option and selling two at a further strike. The extra short option funds the structure, so entry is often at a credit or near zero cost, and that is exactly where the trouble hides: one of the two short options has no long behind it.

The payoff has a sweet spot: profits peak if the underlying drifts to the short strike by expiry. Beyond it, the unhedged short takes over, and the position's risk becomes open-ended on that side, growing with every point the move extends.

Where people get fooled: the free-trade framing. The credit received is the payment for the tail now being carried, and skew often flatters the entry price precisely because the market charges most for the region the seller has agreed to underwrite. The structure profits in the zone the trader expects and is hurt worst by the move the trader ruled out, which is a fragile place to keep an account.
Ratio spread.usage: Used for positions financing a directional view by selling extra options, with the naked component always named explicitly.

Collar.long:
A collar is long stock, a long put below the market, and a short call above it: downside protection funded by surrendering upside. Struck carefully, the call premium covers the put premium and the structure is often described as costless.

Zero net premium is not zero price. The payment happens in forgone rallies above the call strike, and equity returns are concentrated in a minority of strong months, so a standing collar systematically sells the most valuable part of the distribution. Skew adds a quiet tax: the put being bought usually carries higher implied volatility than the call being sold, so the corridor sits tighter or lower than symmetry suggests.

Where people get fooled: reading costless as free. The collar's cost never appears as a debit on the statement; it appears as the rally that was capped, which is easy not to attribute. Over long horizons that invisible cost compounds, and the protection was mostly paid for during the years it was not needed.
Collar.usage: Used when describing bounded equity exposure and hedging structures whose cost is taken in forgone upside rather than cash.

Synthetic position.long:
A synthetic position uses options to replicate another instrument. The canonical case: a long call plus a short put at the same strike and expiry replicates long stock, because whatever happens, one of the two legs delivers the shares at the strike. Put-call parity is the identity that guarantees the equivalence.

The replication is exact in a textbook and approximate at a broker. Differences survive in the details: financing embedded in the option prices, dividends the synthetic does not collect, early assignment risk on the short leg, margin treatment, and pin risk at expiry if spot finishes at the strike.

Where people get fooled: the same payoff for less capital pitch, where the capital saved has quietly become margin requirement and assignment exposure. Two legs mean two spreads crossed, and retail pricing on both frequently costs more than the stock being imitated. Synthetics are genuinely useful for understanding how structures relate; trading them requires the discounts and financing that institutions have and retail does not.
Synthetic position.usage: Used when mapping option structures onto their stock-equivalent exposures and when reasoning through parity relationships.

Put-call parity.long:
Put-call parity is an identity, not a theory: for European options, a call minus a put at the same strike and expiry equals the underlying minus the present value of the strike, adjusted for dividends. It holds because any violation is a riskless profit that someone with cheap financing removes within moments of it appearing.

The identity has practical consequences. It forces calls and puts at the same strike to share one implied volatility. It makes a covered call and a cash-secured put at the same strike the same position. And it means apparent price discrepancies between calls and puts almost always trace to dividends, borrow fees, interest rates or American-style exercise rather than to opportunity.

Where people get fooled: spotting parity violations on a retail screen and reaching for the arbitrage. The gap is usually a hard-to-borrow fee doing exactly what parity predicts, a dividend date, or a stale quote. The identity is the plumbing of option pricing; when it looks broken, the observer is nearly always missing a cost.
Put-call parity.usage: Invoked when relating calls, puts and stock to each other, and when diagnosing why call and put prices differ at a strike.

Poor man's covered call.long:
A poor man's covered call is a diagonal spread dressed as a covered call: a deep in-the-money long-dated call stands in for the stock, and near-dated calls are sold against it. The appeal is capital: the long call costs a fraction of the shares while carrying most of their delta.

The stand-in is imperfect in specific ways. The long call collects no dividends, contains extrinsic value that decays across its life, carries vega the stock does not, and has an expiry date. The short-call overlay keeps the covered call's short-volatility character: capped upside, retained downside.

Where people get fooled: in a sharp decline, the long call's loss as a fraction of capital deployed exceeds the stock's, precisely when less capital at risk was the selling point. The structure is two options, and both legs can go wrong at once: spot down, implied volatility shifting, and the short leg assigned early. It is a legitimate structure with more moving parts than its nickname admits.
Poor man's covered call.usage: Used when discussing capital-efficient covered-call substitutes and the specific ways the substitution differs from owning stock.

Box spread.long:
A box spread combines a long call spread and a short put spread on the same two strikes and expiry. Every path ends with the same fixed payoff, the distance between the strikes, so the structure is a synthetic loan: its price today versus that fixed payout implies an interest rate. Institutions use boxes as a financing tool.

The riskless description carries a load-bearing assumption: European exercise, where nobody can exercise early. On American-style options the box can be dismantled by early assignment, leaving the legs exposed as ordinary short options. In 2019 a retail trader shorted boxes on American-style options believing the position was riskless; early assignment took it apart, and the resulting loss of many times the account is documented and widely cited.

Where people get fooled: risk-free is conditional on exercise style, financing costs and fees, none of which travel from the textbook to a retail account intact. On American options, the same shape is not a loan; it is short options in costume.
Box spread.usage: Discussed as a financing structure and as the standard cautionary example of exercise-style assumptions failing at retail.

Wheel strategy.long:
The wheel sells cash-secured puts until assignment delivers the stock, then sells covered calls against the shares until they are called away, then begins again. Every leg is premium selling, which makes the wheel a short-volatility profile end to end, whatever the cycle metaphor suggests.

The mechanics have a direction built in. Assignment arrives disproportionately in falling markets, so the wheel acquires stock into weakness, often well below the strike. The covered-call phase then caps the recovery. The premiums are collected frequently and are small; the drawdowns are collected rarely and are not.

Where people get fooled: totalling the premiums and calling the sum income while the unrealised loss on assigned stock sits unexamined. The honest benchmark is buying and holding the same names over the same period, and the wheel frequently trails it, with the gap being the price of selling the upside and keeping the downside. Frequent small wins, rare large losses: the wheel does not escape the profile, it repeats it in rotation.
Wheel strategy.usage: Described as a rotation of premium-selling positions, evaluated against simply holding the underlying rather than against zero.

Cash-secured put.long:
A cash-secured put is a short put with the full purchase amount held in reserve: if assigned, the cash buys the shares at the strike. By put-call parity it is the covered call's twin at the same strike, and it shares the same short-volatility profile: the premium is kept in most months, and the large move is absorbed when it comes.

The mechanism has an asymmetry worth stating plainly. The seller keeps the premium when the stock stays up, and receives the stock precisely when it has fallen through the strike, often well through it, because assignment happens after the decline the premium was pricing.

Where people get fooled: the framing of being paid to buy a stock I like at a discount. The discount is measured against the old price, not the new one; the market only delivers the shares once they are worth less than the strike paid. Frequent small premiums, and the occasional gap that assigns far below the strike, is the honest ledger of the yield.
Cash-secured put.usage: Used for premium selling with reserved purchase cash, understood as equivalent to a covered call rather than as a separate, safer idea.

Naked option selling.long:
Naked option selling is shorting options with no offsetting position behind them. Short calls carry unlimited risk upward; short puts carry risk down to zero. The premium collected is the market's price for underwriting that tail, set by participants who have watched it get paid out before.

The return stream is the purest form of the short-volatility profile: frequent small wins, punctuated by rare losses that can exceed the account. The structural cruelty is in the margin: requirements expand exactly as losses mount, so forced liquidation tends to happen at the worst prices of the move. Overnight gaps mean no stop order fences the risk.

Where people get fooled: years of smooth results read as evidence of skill, when they are the collection phase of an insurance book, usually run without reserves. Sellers earn the variance risk premium on average, and the average includes the episodes that return years of premium in days. Anyone selling naked options is an underwriter; most have not priced the policy.
Naked option selling.usage: Used for unhedged short option positions, always described together with the tail and margin behaviour that defines them.

Expected move.long:
The expected move is the amount of movement the options market has priced into a given expiry. The quickest read is the at-the-money straddle: stock at 100, straddle trading at 5, the market is pricing roughly a five-dollar move in either direction. More careful versions blend strikes, but the straddle gets close.

It corresponds to roughly a one standard deviation range, which means finishing outside it is routine rather than remarkable, expected in something like a third of cases. It is a pricing statement, not a boundary.

Where people get fooled: forecasting that a stock moves a lot on earnings is worthless when the expected move already says so, because profit requires the actual move to exceed the priced one. The expected move is the bar the market has set, not the market's prediction coming true. Traders who compare their view against zero movement, instead of against the priced move, are trading against an opponent who was never at the table.
Expected move.usage: Used to read what movement is already priced before an event or expiry, and as the benchmark any movement forecast must clear.

Option chain.long:
The option chain is the listed grid for one underlying: strikes down the side, expiries across, calls on one wing and puts on the other, each row carrying bid, ask, last, volume, open interest, implied volatility and greeks. It is the raw statement of what the options market currently charges for every claim on that underlying.

Liquidity varies enormously inside a single chain. At-the-money strikes in near expiries trade tight and deep; far strikes and distant dates show wide markets, thin size and stale last prints that describe a trade from hours ago, not a price available now.

Where people get fooled: the mid-price on an illiquid row is a fiction nobody is obliged to trade at, and a plan built on chain mids pays the spread twice, entering and exiting. Low open interest means the exit depends on a market maker's quote at the worst possible moment. The chain shows prices; it does not promise them.
Option chain.usage: Used as the reference surface for selecting strikes and expiries, with row-level liquidity checked before any price on it is believed.

Volatility smile.long:
The volatility smile is the curve formed when implied volatility is plotted against strikes for one expiry: the wings sit above the middle, so out-of-the-money options on both sides carry higher IV than at-the-money ones. Currency markets show the symmetric version; equity indices show a tilted one, the skew, with the put wing raised highest.

The shape exists because real return distributions have fat tails that the lognormal assumption underneath flat-volatility pricing does not. The market corrects the model in the only way it can, through prices: extreme strikes are bid to levels that acknowledge extremes happen more often than the textbook says.

Where people get fooled: reading the smile as inefficiency, when it is the market repricing tail probability with better information than the model had. Flattening the curve into a single IV number for the underlying discards exactly the information the smile encodes. Trades that sell the wings because they look expensive are short the tails the smile exists to price.
Volatility smile.usage: Referenced when IV is compared across strikes and when explaining why a single volatility number understates what the market believes.

Gamma pinning.long:
Gamma pinning is the tendency of price, near expiry, to settle toward strikes carrying heavy open interest. The mechanism runs through hedging: dealers long gamma at a strike hedge by buying as price dips below it and selling as it rises above, and that rebalancing dampens movement in the strike's neighbourhood, holding price near it into the close.

This is the better-evidenced cousin of max pain: it proposes actual flows from identifiable participants rather than intent, and academic work has found expiry-day clustering consistent with it. But the effect is conditional on dealers genuinely holding the long-gamma side, which outsiders can only estimate.

Where people get fooled: expecting a pin at every expiry with large open interest, when the sign of dealer positioning decides everything: dealers short gamma at the same strike hedge with the move, and the identical arithmetic repels price rather than anchoring it. Pinning is a tendency under specific positioning, routinely quoted as if it were a law of Fridays.
Gamma pinning.usage: Used for expiry-day price behaviour near heavily held strikes, with dealer positioning named as the conditioning assumption.

Charm and vanna.long:
Charm and vanna are second-order greeks describing how delta itself moves. Charm is delta's drift as time passes with everything else still; vanna is delta's shift as implied volatility changes. For an unhedged holder they are curiosities; for a dealer running a hedged book they are instructions, because every change in delta obliges a rebalancing trade in the underlying.

Aggregated across dealer inventory, those rebalancing flows can be genuine, particularly around large expiries and sharp IV moves, when many books adjust in the same direction at once. Estimating their size, though, requires knowing what dealers hold, which outsiders do not.

Where people get fooled: market commentary invoking vanna and charm flows to explain any drift in either direction, with a confidence the measurement cannot support and no stated condition that would falsify the claim. The effects are real, small, conditional and mostly untradeable at retail. Vocabulary borrowed from a dealing desk is not evidence from one, and sophistication of language is not sophistication of measurement.
Charm and vanna.usage: Mentioned when analysing dealer hedging flows around expiries and volatility shifts, with explicit caveats about observability.

Delta hedging.long:
Delta hedging offsets an option position's directional exposure with the underlying: hold the option, trade the stock against its delta, and rebalance as delta changes. A dealer short a call buys stock as price rises and sells as it falls, buying high and selling low by construction; a hedged long option does the reverse, harvesting movement.

This is the machinery through which options touch the underlying market. Dealer books hedge continuously, so aggregate option positioning translates into mechanical stock flows, which is the foundation under gamma exposure, pinning and squeeze dynamics.

Where people get fooled: delta neutral is not risk neutral. Gamma, vega and gap risk all survive the hedge, and a position hedged flat this morning is directional by lunch. The economics compress into one line: a delta-hedged short option loses money precisely when realised volatility exceeds what implied priced, because the hedging costs scale with movement. Hedging does not remove the volatility bet; it isolates it, which is the entire point and the commonly missed one.
Delta hedging.usage: Used when describing how option exposure is neutralised in the underlying and how dealer hedging transmits option positioning into price.

Volatility as an asset class.long:
Volatility as an asset class means taking exposure to volatility itself as an allocation, rather than as a side effect of other trades. The short side harvests the variance risk premium, running an insurance book that collects steadily and pays out rarely and violently. The long side owns convexity: positions that bleed premium in calm markets and pay off in crises, when everything else in the portfolio is losing.

Each side's cost is the other side's income. Short volatility produces smooth returns with abrupt catastrophic drawdowns; long volatility produces years of steady bleed punctuated by occasional large payoffs that arrive on nobody's schedule.

Where people get fooled: taking either side without accepting its cost as permanent. Short volatility gets mistaken for alpha until the tail arrives and reveals it was always premium for risk carried. Long volatility hedges get trimmed after years of bleeding, frequently just before the event they existed for. The asset class is real; a version of it without the unpleasant half is not on offer.
Volatility as an asset class.usage: Used in allocation discussions where volatility exposure is sized deliberately, with the bleed or the tail named as the accepted cost.

Realised vs implied spread.long:
The realised versus implied spread is the running gap between the volatility options priced and the volatility the underlying then delivered. Measured after the fact, it is the cleanest scorecard for any volatility position: on average implied sits above subsequently realised, and that persistent average gap is the variance risk premium.

For hedged option positions the spread is not context, it is the profit and loss. A delta-hedged short option earns approximately the difference between implied at entry and realised over the holding period; a hedged long pays it. Direction has been hedged away; the spread is what remains.

Where people get fooled: implied is above realised, therefore sell describes the insurance business, not an edge, because the sellers on the other side of history knew the average too. The average conceals the episodes where realised explodes past implied and returns years of collections in a week. The spread is compensation for those episodes, priced by participants with long memories, and collecting it means underwriting them.
Realised vs implied spread.usage: Used as the honest performance measure for volatility trades and the after-the-fact test of what option prices had claimed.
